text.p: Lacklustre base metals meandered in narrow price ranges on the LME on Wednesday, with flagship copper consolidating amid unimpressive volumes.
Gold closed lower on talk of Bundesbank sales while wheat eased on reports of good weather in U.S. growing areas and a slide in soybean prices.
Oil closed slightly firmer after rebounding on technical factors following bearish inventories data.
The CRB index was up 0.08 at 251.38.
Zinc was the best performer in the LME metals complex, touching the $1,340 resistance level on general speculative buying in the afternoon kerb for the second time this week.
Three months zinc finished $2 firmer at $1,339 per tonne.
"Zinc is eroding resistance slowly but surely. Once it closes above $1,340 the next move is $1,400," a trader said.

Copper, by contrast, wrapped up the day $3 easier at $2,414, after failing to regain early highs. Copper prices had initially pushed higher on short covering sparked by a 2,825-tonne LME stock decline. But the pre-market gains faded amid commission house selling and liquidation and never returned.

"The market picked up early but never was able to follow through into a rally. Copper is consolidating its recent gains before resuming to move higher," a trader said. "Volumes were very light all day -- a waste of everyone's time."

Still, analysts and dealers said copper was still on target to conquer the $2,440 resistance level, the high of the year, in coming days. The cash to threes backwardation moved in tandem with three months prices, easing to $53/$57, versus $55/$60.
The other metals were little changed to softer.

Aluminium crumpled towards the $1,650 support level on disappointed liquidation after failing in recent days to breach tough support above $1,670. Traders said it could still ease further towards $1,640 before trying the upside again.

Tin was $5 firmer at $5,730, suggesting that prices were stabilising after recent bouts of producer sales bullied the market, traders said. Nickel, however was $40 lower at $7,730 after general liquidation took its toll.

Lead was unchanged at $622 after bouncing off early lows touched when fund sales triggered sell stops and pushed prices to a low of $615. "Tin, lead and nickel are weary. They're still struggling before any buying is going to come in," a trader said. Alloy was last indicated little changed at $1,515/$1,520.

COMEX gold and silver ended lower Wednesday, after news near the close that some members of the German governing coalition were considering using Bundesbank gold to help Germany meet the criteria for joining the European Monetary Union (EMU).

But NYMEX platinum group metals (PGMs) held onto most of the sessions gains, after palladium saw new contract highs, despite news this week that Russian exports of PGMs would resume in June after a five month suspension.

"Germany is unlikely to actually sell any gold, as it has repeatedly denied it would do so, and is one of the few remaining countries to oppose the sale of IMF gold sales," said Ted Kempf, analyst with New York-based industry consultants, CPM Group. German government sources said Wednesday the government was considering using Bundesbank gold reserves for budgetary purposes, confirming details of a German newspaper report.

COMEX June gold ended down $2.30 an ounce at $348.20, after first ignoring the low-inflation implications of the fall in the U.S. April producer price index of 0.6 percent, and trading up to a session high at $350.80.
In the bullion market, spot gold ended quoted $346.80/30, compared to the London Wednesday afternoon fix at $349.10 an ounce, and the New York close Tuesday around $349.25/75.
COMEX July silver ended down 4.0 cents at $4.838 an ounce, after trading a $4.895-4.830 range.
CBOT soft red winter wheat futures closed lower on a break in soybeans plus overall good wheat crop weather in the U.S. "There was nothing bullish and funds sold it," a trader said.
The USDA said U.S. winter wheat crop conditions improved last week and further improvement was expected this week because of favorable crop weather, industry sources said.
Wheat closed two to 8-1/2 cents per bushel lower, with May down five at $3.83 and July was down 8-1/2 at $3.87.

NYMEX crude ended with slim gains Wednesday, sharply rebounding on short covering after bearish oil inventory data sparked heavy selling that dried up. "Fundamentally, the APIs were bearish. What happened was there was, after a while, a lack of follow-through to the downside, so shorts started to cover," said John Saucer, analyst with Smith Barney in Houston.
June crude ended two cents up at $21.39 a barrel after falling as low as $20.85. Chartists noted technical support for spot crude was found near 20.88 area.
The American Petroleum Institute (API) said that for the week ended May 9, crude stocks grew a whopping 6.94 million barrels. Traders had expected a one million barrel build.

CSCE world sugar futures ended weaker but off the lows in thin dealings, which left many traders wondering just where the market is headed. Benchmark July settled down 0.06 cent per lb at 11.05 cents per lb, having ranged from 11.11 to 10.98 cents.
